introduction.p: An infinite series is defined as the limit of its partial sums. We add the first n terms and ask whether those finite totals converge as n\to\infty. Geometric and telescoping series provide cases where the partial sums can be calculated explicitly.

paragraphs.title: A language point
paragraphs.p: It is common to say “the series \sum a_k converges.” Strictly speaking, the sequence of partial sums converges.
The shorter phrase is harmless once the definition is understood.

p.me: \text{A series converges exactly when its partial sums converge.}

exercise.title: Why is an infinite series a sequence problem in disguise?

statement.p: An infinite series is declared convergent when its sequence of partial sums converges. In your own words, why is that the right definition, and why is it not enough for the individual terms a_n to go to zero?

hint.p: Adding infinitely many numbers has to mean that the running totals settle. Terms going to zero is necessary but can still leave the running totals drifting without bound, as the harmonic series shows.

exercise.title: Why does |r|<1 decide a geometric series?

statement.p: A geometric series converges exactly when |r|<1 (unless the first term is zero). In your own words, why do the powers r^n have to shrink, and what goes wrong when |r|=1 or |r|>1?

hint.p: For a nonzero first term, the finite-sum formula contains a leftover power of the ratio. It vanishes when |r|<1. When |r|\ge1, the terms do not tend to zero. If the first term is zero, every term and every partial sum is zero for any ratio.

exercise.title: Why is cancellation not enough for a telescoping series?

statement.p: In a telescoping series, most terms cancel in the partial sums. In your own words, why is seeing that cancellation only the first step, and why can a series still diverge after a genuine collapse?

hint.p: Cancellation produces a simplified formula for S_n. The series converges only if that simplified leftover still has a limit.

example.title: cancellation does not always mean convergence
example.p: The cancellation was real, but the leftover endpoint still grew without bound.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: For a telescoping series, cancellation is only the first step. The simplified partial sums must still have a limit.

subsection.title: What series add to calculus
subsection.p: A finite sum is arithmetic. An infinite series is calculus because it is a limit:
The preceding examples have explicit formulas for their partial sums.
For many series there is no useful explicit formula for S_n. Convergence tests determine whether the partial sums converge without such a formula.
The first warning is close at hand.
For a series to converge, its terms must get small. But small terms are not enough.
The next section begins with the series
Its terms tend to zero, but its partial sums grow without bound.

exercise.title: Why is an infinite series calculus rather than arithmetic?

statement.p: A finite sum is ordinary addition. An infinite series is defined by \sum a_k=\lim S_n. In your own words, why does that limit make infinite addition a calculus idea, and why will most later series need tests instead of exact formulas for S_n?

hint.p: Geometric and telescoping partial sums simplify explicitly. For other series, a convergence test may be needed instead.

subsection.title: The Cauchy criterion for series
subsection.p: Apply to the partial sums S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k, with S_0=0. The difference of two partial sums is a finite tail.
